**Proof.** Let $h \in H$ and $k \in K$ be arbitrary. Consider the commutator
$$[h,k] \;=\; hkh^{-1}k^{-1}.$$

We use the two factorizations suggested by the hint.

**First factorization.** Write
$$[h,k] \;=\; hkh^{-1}k^{-1} \;=\; (hkh^{-1})\,k^{-1}.$$
Since $K \trianglelefteq G$, conjugation by $h$ sends $K$ into itself, so $hkh^{-1} \in K$. Also $k^{-1} \in K$. Hence the product $(hkh^{-1})k^{-1}$ lies in $K$. Therefore
$$[h,k] \in K.$$

**Second factorization.** Write
$$[h,k] \;=\; hkh^{-1}k^{-1} \;=\; h\,(kh^{-1}k^{-1}).$$
Since $H \trianglelefteq G$, conjugation by $k$ sends $H$ into itself, so $kh^{-1}k^{-1} \in H$. Also $h \in H$. Hence the product $h(kh^{-1}k^{-1})$ lies in $H$. Therefore
$$[h,k] \in H.$$

**Conclusion.** Combining the two inclusions,
$$[h,k] \in H \cap K = \{e\},$$
so $[h,k] = e$, i.e.,
$$hkh^{-1}k^{-1} = e \implies hk = kh.$$

Since $h \in H$ and $k \in K$ were arbitrary, every element of $H$ commutes with every element of $K$. $\blacksquare$
